About: two oscillations on one line, drawn as phasors in a turning frame

Source

Concept
Two oscillations along one line, xa = Aa cos(ωat + φa) and xb = Ab cos(ωbt + φa) with the same phase constant φa = φb = 20° for both (the clock starts with the two in step), added. Top: the Argand diagram in the frame turning with Aa (8 turns per second of t), with Ab drawn head to tail from Aa; the blue arrow runs from the origin to the tip of Ab and its length A is the amplitude of the sum; the dashed circle of radius Ab about the tip of Aa shows every place the tip of the blue arrow can reach. Bottom: x = xa + xb over 4 s between the blue dashed curves ±A(t), with a cursor at the current instant; the height of the envelope at the cursor is the length of the blue arrow.
Controls
Ab (0.25 to 1.50, arbitrary units) and fb (7.00 to 9.00 Hz) set the second oscillation; changing either restarts from t = 0 and runs. ⏸ Pause holds the motion; while paused, the 1/120 s step buttons in the Controls panel or the ← and → keys move t by 1/120 s. ↻ Reset restores Ab = 1.00, fb = 8.50 Hz and t = 0.
Measurement
t is a whole number of 1/120 s steps, shown to three decimals, and the 4 s sweep repeats exactly; at 1× the model's time runs at half the real rate. A is read to two decimals in the Readouts panel.
Serves
Fermi Notes, §4.2 Superposition of Oscillations (Beats; Figs. 50–51): superposition of two oscillations along one line, beats, and phasor addition.
Inquiry
Five questions and a closing summary on how the amplitude A of the sum and the blue arrow behave as Ab and fb are set.
Misconception
Addressed through the answer options of the five questions; left unstated here so that the questions stay open.

Pedagogy principles applied

PrincipleHow this sim honors it
Commit, then compareEach question is answered before its explanation appears; the sim runs freely throughout and nothing is locked.
Operational quantitiest and A are read directly in the Readouts panel; pause and single steps of 1/120 s let the student stop on any instant and read it.
One consistent pictureThe envelope ±A(t) and the blue arrow come from one formula, so the envelope height at the cursor always equals the arrow's length.
What is held fixedAa = 1 and fa = 8.00 Hz never change; only Ab and fb are set.
Honest scalingFrequencies are far below audible so every cycle can be drawn; the half-rate clock is stated in the title band; axes never rescale.
Nothing on screen answers a questionNo marked extreme amplitudes, no beat-period marker, no turn-rate readout and no rotation arrow.
Beats and the Turning Phasor
Phasors and their sum turning frame · x against t, envelope ±A dashed blue · ½ real time at 1×

Guided Inquiry

1 · One turn of the second phasor

With Ab = 1.00 and fb = 8.50 Hz, as at the start, watch the second phasor make one full turn relative to the first. What does the amplitude A of the sum do during that turn?

2 · A shorter second phasor

Ab is now 0.60, with fb = 8.50 Hz. Watch the blue arrow through a full turn of the second phasor, then pause while it is short and use the 1/120 s step buttons until it is as short as it gets. What is the smallest value that the amplitude A of the sum reaches?

3 · Counting the beats

Ab stays at 0.60 and fb is now 9.00 Hz. At 1× the motion runs at half real speed, so count on the t axis of the trace or the t readout: how many times in each second of t does the amplitude A now reach its largest value?

4 · Lowering the second frequency

Keep Ab = 0.60 and lower fb a step at a time from 9.00 Hz, through 8.00 Hz, to 7.00 Hz, watching the second phasor at each setting. What happens to the beats?

5 · A longer second phasor

fb is back at 8.50 Hz and Ab is now 1.50, larger than Aa. What does the blue arrow do during each beat?

6 · What you found

Two oscillations add like two arrows. The second arrow turns relative to the first |fa − fb| times a second, so the amplitude A of the sum swells and shrinks at that beat frequency, between Aa + Ab and |Aa − Ab|.

The sum falls silent only when the amplitudes are equal, and the beats stop when the frequencies are equal.

Beats and the Turning Phasor

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

Two oscillations along one line, with slightly different frequencies, add to a sum whose strength swells and fades again and again. This sim draws each oscillation as a turning arrow and the sum as a third arrow, so you can see where the swelling comes from and how fast it repeats.

What you'll learn

  • How two oscillations of different frequency are added as arrows, head to tail.
  • How the amplitude A of the sum depends on the amplitude Ab and the frequency fb of the second oscillation.
  • How the beat frequency follows from the two frequencies, and how to read it off the t axis.
  • How the envelope ±A(t) and the length of the blue arrow are one quantity.
The set-up: Aa and Ab added head to tail, and the sum A from the origin to the tip of Ab.

What's on screen

  • Dark arrows (top): Aa, and Ab drawn head to tail from its tip, in a frame that turns with Aa.
  • Blue arrow: from the origin to the tip of Ab. Its length A is the amplitude of the sum.
  • Dashed circle: radius Ab, centred on the tip of Aa. It shows every place the tip of the blue arrow can reach.
  • Trace x = xa + xb (bottom), between the blue dashed envelope ±A(t), with a cursor at the present instant.
  • Readouts: Time t and Amplitude A.
See itLet the run start again from t = 0 with your current settings. Watch for: the blue arrow changing length as the second arrow turns, while the cursor sweeps along the trace below.

03

Two oscillations are two turning arrows

Each oscillation, xa = Aa cos(2πfat + φ) and xb = Ab cos(2πfbt + φ), is the horizontal shadow of an arrow of length Aa or Ab turning at fa or fb turns a second. In the sim φ = 20° for both.

Draw them in a frame that turns with Aa (the sim's frame, 8 turns a second). Then Aa stands still and Ab turns relative to it, at fb − fa turns a second. Added head to tail, they give the blue arrow, and its length is the amplitude A of the sum.

Notes (4.11). The bracket is the blue arrow; the factor in front is the fast turning that the frame removes.
The sim's picture (notes, Figure 50). Δφ = (ωb − ωa)t is how far Ab has turned from Aa. The tip of the blue arrow stays on the dashed circle.

The envelope ±A(t) under the phasors is the length of the blue arrow, drawn against t.

See itRestart the run from t = 0 and follow the blue arrow. Watch for: the tip of the blue arrow staying on the dashed circle while the second arrow turns.
04

Silence needs equal arrows

A is largest, Aa + Ab, when Ab points the same way as Aa, and smallest, |Aa − Ab|, when it points the opposite way. Equation (4.12) says the same, with the cosine running between +1 and −1.

Notes (4.12): the length of the blue arrow, by the cosine rule.

A reaches zero only if the dashed circle passes through the origin, and that happens only when Ab = Aa. Then A = 0 for an instant, once in each beat. With Ab = 0.60 the circle misses the origin and A bottoms out at 0.40, so the sum never falls silent.

The same Aa, three lengths of Ab. The blue mark is the shortest A the sum ever reaches.
See itSet the second arrow equal to the first, Ab = 1.00. Watch for: A reading 0.00 for an instant as the blue arrow shrinks to a point.
See itShorten it to Ab = 0.60. Watch for: A never dropping below 0.40.
05

A longer second arrow circles the origin

If Ab is longer than Aa, the dashed circle encloses the origin. The blue arrow can then never shrink to nothing: it stays at least Ab − Aa long, and it turns all the way round the origin once in each beat. With Ab = 1.50, A runs from 0.50 to 2.50.

If Ab is shorter than Aa, the origin lies outside the circle. The blue arrow only swings to either side of Aa, by at most arcsin(Ab/Aa), which is 37° for Ab = 0.60.

Both are the same sum of two arrows. Which behaviour you get depends only on which arrow is longer.

See itLengthen the second arrow to Ab = 1.50, longer than Aa. Watch for: the blue arrow turning all the way round the origin, with A never below 0.50.
06

Beats come at the difference frequency

A is largest each time Ab has gained one full turn on Aa, and it gains |fb − fa| turns a second. So A peaks |fa − fb| times a second: the beat frequency. At fb = 8.50 Hz the peaks are 2 s apart in t; at fb = 9.00 Hz, 1 s apart.

The notes' form for equal amplitudes has a half in the slow cosine. The amplitude is its modulus, 2Aa|cos½(ωa − ωb)t|, and |cos| repeats each time its argument grows by π, not 2π. The peaks are therefore 2π/|ωa − ωb| apart, and the half does not change the beat rate.

Notes (4.10), equal amplitudes. The slow cosine carries the envelope; the fast one runs at the mean frequency.
x = xa + xb for Ab = 0.60 and fb = 9.00 Hz, between the envelope ±A(t). The fast oscillation inside keeps, on average, the frequency of the larger oscillation, 8.00 Hz here; it runs at the mean frequency, 8.50 Hz, only when Ab = Aa.
See itSet Ab = 0.60 and fb = 9.00 Hz. Watch for: A peaking once every second of t. At 1× the sim runs at half real speed, so that is every 2 s on the clock.
07

Beats stop when the frequencies match

Lower fb towards fa and the beats slow down, because Ab gains fewer turns a second. At fb = 8.00 Hz it gains none: the arrows stay in line, A stays at Aa + Ab, and nothing swells or fades.

Go below 8.00 Hz and Ab turns the other way round. The beats return at |fa − fb|, the same rate as the same distance above: 1.00 Hz at both 7.00 Hz and 9.00 Hz.

The notes call the slowly changing amplitude a valid description when |ωa − ωb| is much smaller than ωa. In the sim |fa − fb| is at most 1.00 Hz, against fa = 8.00 Hz.

See itSet fb = 8.00 Hz. Watch for: the second arrow standing still and A fixed at Aa + Ab.
See itSet fb = 7.00 Hz. Watch for: the second arrow turning the other way, clockwise, with beats back at 1.00 Hz.
08

Where it matters

  • Tuning forks. Two forks of nearly equal frequency, sounded together, are heard as one tone whose loudness swells and dies away |fa − fb| times a second.
  • Tuning a piano. A tuner listens for beats between a string and a reference tone, and adjusts the string until they slow to a stop: the sim's fb = fa.
  • Coupled pendulums. The slow exchange of energy between two weakly coupled pendulums (notes, Section 2.1) is the same effect, with the two normal-mode frequencies as ωa and ωb.
Go deeper: why the sim uses 8 Hz

Real tones are hundreds of hertz. The sim uses 8 Hz so that every cycle can be drawn. Only the difference sets the beat, so 440 Hz against 441 Hz beats at 1.00 Hz, just like fb = 9.00 Hz here.

09

Summary

In one line. Each oscillation is a turning arrow, and the length of the sum, drawn from the origin to the tip of the second arrow, is the amplitude A that the sim reads out.

Key points

  • A is the length of the blue arrow, and the height of the envelope ±A(t).
  • If Ab is longer, the blue arrow circles the origin once a beat; if shorter, it only swings to either side of Aa.
  • A reaches zero only when Ab = Aa, and the beats stop at fb = fa.

Common mix-ups

  • “Equal amplitudes keep A = 2.” A = 2 only when the arrows are in line. Half a beat later A = 0.
  • “Beats always fall silent once a cycle.” Only when Ab = Aa. At Ab = 0.60 the quietest A is 0.40.
  • “The ½ in (4.10) halves the beat rate.” The modulus restores it: at fb = 9.00 Hz, A peaks once a second.

Things to try on your own

  • Set Ab = 1.25, pause, and use the 1/120 s buttons to find the largest and smallest A. Compare them with Aa ± Ab.
  • Set fb = 8.75 Hz and measure the time between two peaks of A on the t axis. Compare it with 1/|fa − fb|.
  • At the same Ab, compare fb = 7.50 Hz with 8.50 Hz and note which way the second arrow turns in each.
